Beyond the mere creation of Dirac cone replicas, the effect of this interaction on photoemission measurements is poorly understood. We utilized synchrotron radiation for photon-energy-dependent angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to investigate the complex final-state interactions of photoelectrons within the heterostructure of monolayer graphene, ZLG, and SiC. We identify multiple resonances in the photoemission intensity of the Dirac cone as a function of photon energy that originate from interlayer interference, confirmed with a multiple scattering model. We also demonstrate for the first time that the relative intensity of the replica bands induced by the $(6\sqrt{3} \times 6\sqrt{3})\text{R}30^\circ$ reconstruction scales with the electron kinetic energy. Finally, we resolved four nondispersing electronic states, which originate from the ZLG. Our findings show that the three-dimensional (3D) structure of SiC and ZLG manifests itself in the photoemission from two-dimensional (2D) epitaxial graphene. By revealing how 3D substrate architecture dictates the photoemission of a 2D layer, this work establishes a crucial framework for investigating the electronic structure of complex heterostructures via ARPES.

title: Damped polarizability and first hyperpolarizability of large systems with hybrid functionals: self-consistent and Lanczos solvers
abstract: We present a damped coupled-perturbed Kohn-Sham method to compute the dynamical polarizability and first hyperpolarizability of finite systems, implemented in the CRYSTAL code for semi-local, global and range-separated hybrid functionals. The approach is based on the adiabatic time-dependent density functional theory for the complex-valued (hyper)polarizabilities, describing optical phenomena such as absorption, and the nonlinear second-harmonic generation, rectification and Pockels effect. These are obtained either at individual frequencies with a self-consistent solver based on Pulay extrapolation, or at an arbitrary grid of frequency and damping factors with a Lanczos solver, from which the first-order amplitudes required in the hyperpolarizability can be reconstructed. With hybrid functionals, the self-consistent solver tends to become impractical at some point beyond the absorption onset, where there are many excitations for which the external frequency lies between their energy and those of their contributing single-particle transitions, and its convergence eventually stalls for large systems. In contrast, the convergence of the Lanczos method is essentially independent of size, hence the cost of the dynamical response calculation scales with system size as the hybrid ground-state calculation. The implementation is validated in a small molecule and, as an application, we study the first and second-order optical response of a series of hexagonal boron nitride flakes of up to 324 atoms. The use of range-separated hybrid functionals allows to capture the strongly-bound first excitation of the monolayer, and evidences the failure of the self-consistent method to converge excitations with strong electron-hole attraction.

title: GibbScope: interactive calculation and visualization of phase diagrams in the browser
abstract: Phase diagrams are a constant work in progress as Gibbs-energy models are fitted, revised, and disputed in the light of an endless stream of experimental and computational data. Yet, phase diagrams are still largely communicated as static figures, in much the same way as a century ago. We present GibbScope, a web-based framework for interactive calculation and visualization of binary phase diagrams. Written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly, the new CALPHAD engine recomputes a complete phase diagram in the browser in a fraction of a second with zero installation on the user or server side. The high speed allows new ways of interacting with phase diagrams and underlying assessments. Validation against well-established CALPHAD software shows agreement to within 0.01 K for invariant temperatures and within 1e-6 for tie-line compositions for most databases. GibbScope offers interactive CALPHAD parameter adjustments, overlays of different assessments and point-by-point misfit to experimental data, which makes the diagram a live, working object. In addition, GibbScope provides convenient access to 2745 thermodynamic databases from the SGTE collection (Hallstedt, 2025) and their live adjustment. For over 1200 of these databases, all phases are modeled in full with the current implementation.

title: Harmonic origin of local symmetry breaking in PbTe revealed using machine-learned potentials
abstract: We use machine-learned interatomic potentials combined with higher-order interatomic force constant models to show that finite-range polar correlations in PbTe are driven by long-range harmonic interactions rather than lattice anharmonicity. Our molecular dynamics simulations reveal a spatial polar correlation range exceeding 50 Å at low temperatures and decreasing with increasing temperature. Selective interatomic force constant mapping demonstrates that crystal anharmonicity usually associated with the formation of polar nanoregions suppresses polar correlations. Instead, long-range harmonic interactions extending to 13 Å are necessary to reproduce the spatial coherence of local dipoles. In reciprocal space, these extended harmonic interactions correspond to high curvature of the transverse optical (TO) phonon branch at the $Γ$ point. Comparison with isostructural NaCl connects these extended interactions to local underscreening of predominantly Coulombic forces. Our results provide a key microscopic description of finite-range polar correlations and a framework for understanding local symmetry breaking in centrosymmetric materials.

title: Ab Initio Molecular Dynamics-Guided Machine-Learning Potentials for Mapping Nitric Oxide Interactions with Oxygen-Covered Graphite
abstract: Exploratory ab initio molecular dynamics is used to construct machine-learning interatomic potentials for NO interactions with highly oriented pyrolytic graphite at 33\% bridge-site oxygen coverage. Representative configurations sampled across surface temperatures and incidence energies provide reference energies and forces for training and validation. The selected potential enables relaxation of 300 adsorption configurations and construction of spatial and angular interaction maps. These maps reveal increasingly restricted attractive regions during vertical approach and reduced short-range repulsion upon molecular reorientation. The resulting adsorption geometries and interaction landscapes guide further first-principles sampling toward refining potentials for NO oxidation dynamics.

title: Quantum benchmarks for magnetic energies and transition temperatures
abstract: Predicting magnetic ordering temperatures requires accurate exchange interactions and an appropriate treatment of spin thermodynamics. Here we assess these requirements through complementary quantum Monte Carlo benchmarks. For five insulating antiferromagnets, we compare ferromagnetic-antiferromagnetic energy differences from diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) and density functional theory with references reconstructed from inelastic neutron scattering (INS) exchanges. DMC underestimates these references but achieves a mean absolute error comparable to the best-performing functionals tested. Separately, we directly test the previously proposed (S+1)/S rescaling of classical Monte Carlo temperatures against quantum stochastic series expansion simulations for 17 compounds using corresponding INS-derived Heisenberg Hamiltonians. Rescaling reduces the mean absolute classical-quantum temperature difference from 81.7 to 8.2 K, with a mean absolute percentage difference of 5.9 %. These results establish a direct quantum benchmark for the rescaling within the tested models and emphasize that improvements in electronic magnetic energy scales should be accompanied by attention to quantum spin thermodynamics.

title: The Weight Is in the Reading: Hidden States in Memristors, Memlumors, and Electrochemical Transistors
abstract: Physical synapses are routinely described by a single number, the weight, that is identified with a conductance, a current, or a luminescence yield. This identification conflates two different objects: the internal state that the device stores, and the signal obtained when that state is read. Building on Chua's formulation of memristive systems, we separate the state variable, which evolves with the excitation history, from the observation map that converts it into a measured signal, and we define the weight as the outcome of a specified read protocol. Three platforms show the consequences: a memristor, in which the same voltage writes and reads; a memlumor, in which light both modifies the state and produces the photoluminescence that reports it; and an organic electrochemical transistor (OECT), in which the gate writes and the channel reads. In the transistor, two states prepared by different histories give the same channel current at a specific drain bias and become distinguishable again when the bias is changed, while the stored charge persists and the gate current continues to separate them. Published experiments provide precedents: a drain-bias-dependent cancellation of the OECT transient, and trapped charges in perovskite memlumors that are invisible to conventional time-resolved photoluminescence but revealed by a read-write-read sequence. A synaptic weight is therefore not a property of the material alone but of the material together with its readout, and reports of synaptic behavior should specify what is stored, what is measured, and how one is inferred from the other.

title: Neutronic Field-Effect Transistor
abstract: Field-effect electronic devices are in widespread use in communication, computing, data storage, and sensing applications. We demonstrate a neutronic field-effect transistor (NFET) that is analogous to the Datta-Das electron spin transistor and atomtronic devices. The NFET is based on a perfect-crystal Mach-Zehnder neutron interferometer with phase shifts applied to the spin and path degrees of freedom.

title: Spin-valve effect through electrostatic coupling
abstract: We propose a spin-valve effect in which an insulating magnetic van der Waals multilayer controls the conductance of an adjacent non-magnetic conductor by electrostatic coupling, without transport-electrons entering the magnetic layers. The coupling is induced by the variations of the electronic structure when the relative orientation of the magnetization of adjacent monolayers changes from parallel to antiparallel, modifying both the dielectric constant and band alignment. We consider two types of coupling and device concepts: charge transfer to a graphene monolayer and capacitive coupling in a single-electron transistor. We use density functional calculations to assess the magnitude of the effect in various materials, including CrI$_3$, CrBr$_3$, CrCl$_3$ and NiBr$_2$. We predict magnetoresistance ratios in the range of 1.14-1.20 for the charge-transfer device and up to $10^3$ in the single-electron transistor.

title: Scalable operating currents in amorphous W-N/FePt superconducting rectifiers
abstract: We demonstrate high-efficiency, field-free superconducting diode behavior in W-N/FePt bilayers fabricated entirely by sputtering at room temperature. The devices combine amorphous W-N superconducting thin films with a 48-nm-thick FePt layer exhibiting remanent stripe-domain magnetization. We used lithographically patterned microbridges to compare W-N/FePt bilayers with single-layer W-N reference films at three nominal W-N thicknesses (18, 24, and 28 nm). The bilayers exhibit superconducting transition temperatures of approximately 4.1-4.3 K. At zero applied magnetic field, the current-voltage (I-V) characteristics exhibit pronounced nonreciprocity, controlled by the orientation of the in-plane remanent FePt magnetization relative to the transport current. The diode response is maximized for perpendicular alignment, reverses polarity upon magnetization reversal, and is strongly suppressed when the magnetization is aligned with the current. This behavior is consistent with asymmetric vortex entry and motion governed by the magnetic stray fields generated near the bridge edges. At 3 K with the remanent magnetization perpendicular to the current, increasing the W-N thickness from 18 to 28 nm widens the current interval between the dissipation thresholds for opposite polarities from about 0.3 to 1.55 mA. All three bilayers exhibit diode efficiencies of approximately 75-80% in this configuration.

title: Mechanisms of Zener diode and ohmic contact resulting from a heavily doped p-n junction: A novel explanation in terms of impurity-photovoltaic-effect resulting from infrared self-emission at room-temperature
abstract: In textbooks, a quantum-mechanical tunneling mechanism based on electron-wavefunction is used to explain Zener diode as well as ohmic contact resulting from a heavily doped p-n junction. In this study, an attempt in particle description is made to explain these devices. Any object at room-temperature emits infrared (IR) photons. The process of heavy doping can cause many defects. The self-absorption of the IR emission could be achieved through sub-band-gap excitations due to defects, creating carriers. In a heavily doped p-n junction device, some of the IR-generated carriers diffuse into the junction which has a built-in field. The built-in field sweeps out the carriers, creating IR photocurrent. The reverse leakage current of the p-n junction is regarded as the IR photocurrent according to a precedent where impurity-photovoltaic-effect is used to explain circuit devices (arXiv:2510.18226). Heavy doping results in not only a great many IR-generated carriers but also an avalanche effect at low voltage, producing Zener breakdown. Additionally, the impurity-photovoltaic-effect can make a reasonable contribution to explaining the temperature dependence of Zener breakdown. If the doping is very heavy, the heavily doped p-n junction can be altered to create an ohmic contact, which can also be explained in terms of impurity-photovoltaic-effect. Not only quantum mechanics, but also this photovoltaic mechanism in particle description can explain the above devices. Considering the wave-particle duality, the combination of quantum-mechanical and photovoltaic mechanisms is suggested to explain these devices. Each mechanism plays a big or small role in the explanation.

title: Why fluid relaxation modes matter: Nonlinear frequency response, dynamical integrity, and dynamic pull-in of electrostatic microbeams with squeeze-film damping
abstract: The squeeze film between an electrostatically actuated microbeam can both induce damping and add stiffness to the structure. In addition, the dynamics of the film can interact with the nonlinear response of the microbeam. This paper extends a reduced-order model built on the complex modes of the coupled fluid-structure problem to the computation of periodic responses and their stability for clamped-clamped microbeams. Periodic orbits are continued in the frequency domain, and their stability is determined from their Floquet multipliers. The robustness of the response is assessed through basins of attraction, integrity measures, and dynamic pull-in maps in the plane of the excitation parameters. The model is validated against the measured and computed frequency response of a microswitch. Closed-form expressions are derived for the fluid relaxation modes, together with a correction for strongly coupled films, and define a parameter that characterizes the regime of the film. The approach is applied to different microbeams including cases where fluid modes relax on the timescale of the oscillation. For all simulated devices, a single fluid mode is necessary and sufficient, whereas adding coupled modes cannot replace it, whether the fluid modes respond quasi-statically or carry their own dynamics. Removing the fluid mode displaces both bifurcations that bound the pull-in band, changes the size of the basins of attraction and the position of the attractor within them, misses an abrupt erosion of the safe basin under increasing excitation, and shifts the whole region of dynamic pull-in in the excitation plane. The reduced model, with three real unknowns, makes these global analyses affordable for a fully coupled fluid-structure system.

title: Analytical Framework Relating Capacitance-Frequency Measurements and Hysteresis in Perovskite Solar Cells
abstract: Mobile ion migration strongly influences the electrical response and current-voltage hysteresis of perovskite solar cells. However, quantitative determination of ionic transport parameters typically requires transient measurements, extensive numerical simulations, and/or fitting procedures involving multiple uncertain parameters. Here, we present an analytical model that establishes a direct relationship between capacitance-frequency (C-f) characteristics and ionic transport properties in perovskite solar cells, while accounting for interlayer effects. The model describes the transition from the ion-screened depletion capacitance at low frequencies to the geometric capacitance at high frequencies and demonstrates that the characteristic transition frequency provides a direct measure of the dielectric relaxation time for ions. Furthermore, the model establishes a quantitative connection between C-f characteristics and scan-rate-dependent current-voltage hysteresis, enabling prediction of the scan-rate window in which maximum hysteresis occurs. Drift-diffusion simulations show excellent agreement with the analytical predictions over wide ranges of ion density, ion mobility, transport-layer mobility and doping concentration. Experimental measurements confirm the predicted correlation between capacitance and hysteresis. By providing a direct, physically transparent, and computationally efficient route for extracting ionic transport parameters from routine impedance measurements, this work offers a practical tool for quantifying ion migration and understanding dynamic phenomena in perovskite solar cells.

title: Split-Ring Couplers for On-Skin Wi-Fi Communication via an SSPP Waveguide Textile
abstract: Textile spoof surface plasmon polariton (SSPP) waveguides offer guided on-body links, but their body-facing ground conductors obstruct coupling from on-skin wireless nodes. This letter presents a split-ring coupling interface using local ground recesses at the textile terminations, without patterned garment-side launchers. The capacitively loaded rings are supported by polydimethylsiloxane carriers with a thickness of 2~mm. An image-current model and full-wave simulations examine the effect of backing-ground spacing and determine the recess geometry. For a 450~mm textile waveguide on a water-filled body phantom, the measured $S_{21}$ at 2.45 GHz was $-$18.8~dB, versus $-$60.9~dB without the textile. A 625-position scan showed a maximum 5.1 dB reduction relative to the nominal position within the measured joint $\pm$5~mm placement region. A separate two-node IEEE~802.11n test demonstrated a 65~Mb/s physical-layer (PHY) rate with zero packet errors among 300 frames at $-$20~dBm transmit power through the coupler link. These results establish high-rate, placement-tolerant on-skin Wi-Fi communication through an SSPP waveguide textile.

title: Enhancing valley splitting in Si/SiGe Wiggle Well quantum dots through integrated stressor-gate architectures
abstract: Engineering large and reproducible valley splittings is essential for the scalable operation of silicon spin qubits. In Si/SiGe quantum dot devices, valley splitting arises predominantly from atomic-scale disorder and is therefore inherently random, motivating approaches that introduce a large deterministic contribution. Strain-assisted Wiggle Wells provide a route to deterministic valley splitting by combining an oscillatory Ge concentration in the Si well with shear strain; however, generating the required strain in a manner compatible with large-scale architectures remains a challenge. Here, we propose patterned stressed thin films as a scalable approach for generating shear strain in the quantum well of Si/SiGe quantum dot devices. Finite-element simulations show that compressively stressed TiN films can generate shear strains exceeding 0.1\% at the quantum well, sufficient for deterministic valley splittings of hundreds of $μ\text{eV}$ in strain-assisted Wiggle Wells. We show that this strain can extend across multiple quantum dots and is maintained in realistic gate geometries, providing a fabrication-compatible approach for scaling deterministic valley splitting to quantum dot arrays.

title: Universal semiclassical drift velocity of magnetic edge channels
abstract: Magnetic edge channels, arising at the edge of a two-dimensional electron gas in a magnetic field, are topologically protected and propagate unidirectionally along the edge. Their group velocities at the Fermi level, being averaged harmonically, result in drift velocity, which is related to the edge density of states, quantum capacitance, and the velocity of edge magnetoplasmons. Using semiclassical quantization of electron skipping orbits, we show that the drift velocity equals 1/2 of the electron Fermi velocity in the limit of a large number of edge channels crossing the Fermi level. This result, being universal for a hard edge and for isotropic dispersion, is checked numerically for massive electrons and for massless electrons in graphene. The drift velocity at smooth electrostatically defined edges lacks such universality. In the case of anisotropic dispersion, the semiclassical drift velocity at the hard edge reduces to a coordinate-velocity correlation along the cyclotron orbit.

title: Spin Shuttling Through Quantum-Dot Based Chiral Molecular Bridges: Gauge Constraints, Holonomy, and Quantum Gates
abstract: Chiral molecular bridges between silicon quantum dots can provide novel two-qubit entangling resources via the chirality-induced spin-selectivity (CISS) effect. We evaluate this using Makhlin invariants. Modeling a phase-coherent bridge as an $\mathrm{SU}(2)$-valued hopping between two spins, a Schrieffer-Wolff reduction yields a twisted exchange interaction $J \mathbf{S}_1 \cdot \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S}_2$, whose Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya and symmetric anisotropic parts are fixed by a single bridge angle $α$. Using the Kaplan-Shekhtman-Entin-Wohlman-Aharony (KSEA) gauge argument, we prove this interaction is locally equivalent to isotropic exchange; thus, a single chiral bond does not constitute a new entangling class. Breaking this gauge symmetry reveals genuine chiral utility: chiral exchange converts a uniform transverse field into a synthetic gradient, bringing the two-qubit propagator within $7\times10^{-4}$ of the CNOT class in invariant space 4.7 times faster than an equivalent orthogonal gradient. Shuttling a spin through bridges with non-collinear axes implements a non-Abelian $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ holonomy, yielding rotationally non-reciprocal transport and closed-loop geometric gates that suppress dynamical-phase noise to second order. To address the unsettled microscopic origin of CISS, we introduce a unified transport channel combining coherent rotation, a direction-reversing spin filter, and pointer-basis dephasing. This model obeys an exact $\tanh$ composition law for pumped polarization and a closed-form transverse decay law, yielding four observables that experimentally over-determine the bridge's coherent fraction $F_c$. Finally, we quantify silicon-specific hardware constraints, establishing the Landau-Zener valley-adiabaticity window ($E_v \geq 2.1\sqrt{\hbar v}$) and charge-noise limit ($σ_J/J \leq 3\%$) required for $99\%$ gate fidelity.

title: Compensation Domain Walls in Ferrimagnets as Spin-Torque Oscillator Candidates
abstract: Spin-torque nano-oscillators are promising nanoscale microwave sources, yet their performance is often limited by narrow operational ranges and sensitivity to device parameters. Here, we numerically investigate the dynamics of compensation domain walls in ferrimagnetic systems driven by spin-transfer torque as a microwave source candidate. These walls arise in structures with adjacent regions of different compensation character, where the competition between exchange and Zeeman energies under an applied magnetic field stabilizes a distinct magnetic texture. We demonstrate steady current-driven rotation of compensation domain walls over a broad range of current densities within the model. To elucidate the underlying mechanism, we develop a collective-coordinate model and derive an analytical expression for the oscillation frequency, which quantitatively reproduces the dependence on current and magnetic field observed in micromagnetic simulations. Our results identify compensation domain walls as a candidate platform for tunable spin-torque nano-oscillators with intrinsic field-induced confinement.

title: All-to-all connectivity via adiabatic ZZ interactions in a superconducting flux qubit processor
abstract: Scalable superconducting quantum processors would benefit from high qubit connectivity, yet existing architectures connect neighbouring qubits via tunable couplers, which introduce substantial wiring and control overhead. Here, we propose a baseband-driven adiabatic ZZ gate that entangles any selected pair in a register of flux qubits coupled via a common cavity. The qubits stay dc-biased at their flux sweet spot. Strong drives applied selectively through local flux lines, at frequencies far below the qubit transitions, adiabatically tilt the quantization axes and generate an effective longitudinal ZZ interaction. The strength of the coupling is tunable and controlled by the amplitudes and relative phase of the drives rather than by any resonance condition. Numerical simulations give coherent gate errors below $10^{-4}$ over broad ranges of drive frequency, with comparable fidelities for two simultaneous gates in a four-qubit register. The protocol is robust against frequency fluctuations and remains effective even when many qubits are coupled to the cavity.

title: Quotient Index for Symmetry-Protected Zeros and the Tenfold Way in Mackey's Construction of Super Corepresentations
abstract: Symmetries that anticommute with a Hamiltonian can protect zero modes by obstructing their removal through symmetry-compatible perturbations. We formulate this obstruction as a quotient of the additive group of symmetry representations by the image of the map that forgets a compatible representation grading. To compute the quotient, we use Mackey's method to construct all irreducible super corepresentations of finite graded symmetry groups, allowing antiunitary operations and projective factor systems. Starting from the unitary Hamiltonian-preserving normal subgroup, this construction yields two complex and ten real structural types, characterized by residual Altland--Zirnbauer symmetry algebras. The residual and induced graded modules have isomorphic graded commutants, and their represented symmetry algebras share a graded Morita class that is super opposite to that of the commutant. We derive character criteria that identify these types. Exhaustive enumeration of the restriction relations gives independent sector contributions $0$, $Z$, or $Z_2$, with only integer factors in the purely unitary case. In the finite semisimple setting, the complete index vanishes if and only if all zero modes can be lifted by a symmetry-compatible perturbation. Applications to one-dimensional end states and interpolation cylinders of disordered boundary Dirac theories recover protected multiplet counts and connect the quotient to bulk topology and sigma-model topological terms using bulk--boundary correspondence, texture-index theorems, and fermion-phase calculations.

title: Direct imaging of vortex lattices across fractional fillings in two-dimensional Josephson junction arrays
abstract: Josephson junction arrays are predicted to host a rich sequence of commensurate vortex lattices. However, direct imaging of these configurations remains limited, while transport measurements cannot resolve the underlying vortex arrangements or how order breaks down. Using scanning superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) microscopy, we resolve individual vortices and directly image this long-predicted hierarchy spanning filling factors $f$ = 1/8 to 1/2 in two-dimensional Au-Nb Josephson junction arrays, including several states with no discernible transport signatures. At $f$ = 1/4, two structurally distinct vortex orders with 4$\times$4 and 2$\times$4 unit cells coexist, consistent with their energetic degeneracy in the frustrated XY model. Away from commensurate filling, we resolve defect structures tied to the underlying vortex-lattice order: the $f$ = 1/2 checkerboard retains its order around isolated excess vortices and vacancies, whereas the $f$ = 1/3 staircase fragments into domains separated by domain walls. These results reveal how frustration, competing configurations, and defects shape the spatial coherence of commensurate vortex order in engineered superconducting lattices.

title: DreamLander: A 6-DOF World Model based Reinforcement Learning Planetary Lander
abstract: Soft powered descent landings are becoming evermore important in the field of space exploration and scientific advancement, because of their ability to deliver mission critical payloads, both highly accurately and safely. The high efficiency restriction on planetary landings due to the severely limited fuel supply results in the need for optimal guidance trajectories and control. Model based reinforcement learning is proving to be an important tool in simplifying the highly complex process of generating optimal guidance trajectories and control. In this work, we present DreamLander, a state of the art model based reinforcement learning algorithm based on DreamerV3, to generate optimal guidance and control for a realistic 6 degree of freedom entry descent landing problem. The model based approach creates a sample efficient and highly generalizable model that can be applied to a variety of scenarios whilst maintaining a high degree of accuracy, landing within 2 meters of the designated landing zone, and with velocity norm less than 0.3 meters per second. DreamLander makes use of state sensor observations, making progress toward End-to-End solutions of the Entry Descent Landing problem.

title: Simulating Vein Compressibility for Ultrasound-Guided Femoral Access: Speed, Accuracy, and Phantom Validation
abstract: In ultrasound-guided femoral access, probe pressure deforms the tissue and changes the vascular anatomy a robot observes. A simulator must reproduce these mechanics fast enough for robotic interaction, yet the computational effort needed for a clinically meaningful signal like vein collapse before artery is unclear. We test the feasibility of a physics-based simulation in NVIDIA's Isaac Sim for Healthcare, with Stable Neo-Hookean tissue solved by Vertex Block Descent on one GPU. A simulation of a low-fidelity cylindrical benchtop phantom with known geometry and mechanical properties, pressed by a robot, predicted its artery within 5 percentage points at every depth. It matched the vein within 3 points through 11 mm of a 25.4 mm press and followed the collapse behavior of the low-fidelity physical phantom. Across element size, time step, and solver iterations, wall clock time per frame scaled linearly with solver work, but accuracy did not improve with more work. The chosen setting reduced solver time per frame by a factor of 976, from 29,700 ms to 30.4 ms, while remaining within 1.03 points of the finest reference setting. The physics solver alone took 30.4 ms per frame, while the full stack, including ultrasound and graphics rendering, took 56.4 ms per frame. Finally, when seeded with realistic literature-based mechanical properties, the digital leg model compressed the vein far more than the artery at every setting, reproducing the expected clinical signal of vein collapse before artery, which is used to distinguish them. In total, these results suggest that the NVIDIA Isaac Sim platform may be suitable for augmenting reinforcement learning training or online simulation for autonomous femoral access with ultrasound.

title: Learning Heterogeneous Tactile Representation for General Dexterous Manipulation
abstract: Tactile sensing is an indispensable modality for contact-rich dexterous manipulation, a capability that hints at the ultimate frontiers of embodied intelligence. However, commercially available tactile sensors are still at a relatively early stage of development, with each type of sensor offering irreplaceable strengths alongside its own drawbacks. A key challenge is thus to free tactile understanding from sensor-specific physics, so that embodied models can effectively leverage heterogeneous tactile data. To this end, we develop LingBot-Touch, a tactile foundation model characterized by the following properties. (i) Our model yields a unified representation across different tactile sensors (i.e., piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors), and is easily extensible to new sensor types. (ii) The resulting tactile tokens are plug-and-play: they can be seamlessly integrated into policy models across paradigms, from diffusion policy to vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_{0.5}$ and LingBot-VLA, consistently enhancing manipulation dexterity. (iii) Extensive experiments, spanning simulation and real-robot deployments across multiple hardware platforms, demonstrate that our tactile representation substantially benefits complex manipulation tasks while maintaining strong computational efficiency. We believe the findings in this work demonstrate the potential of leveraging cross-sensor data to scale tactile learning, and offer encouraging insights for the design of future hardware and embodied models.

title: Distributed Global Pose Synchronization for Heterogeneous Multiple Rigid Body Systems on SE(3)
abstract: This paper addresses the problem of global pose synchronization for heterogeneous multiple rigid-body systems evolving on the matrix Lie group $\SE(3)$. We first construct a new potential function on $\SE(3) \times \mathbb{R}$ with a generalized non-diagonal weighting matrix, together with a set of switching variables governed by continuous-discrete hybrid dynamics. Based on this new potential function and these switching variables, we propose a distributed hybrid feedback control scheme that uses relative pose on $\SE(3)$ and group velocity measurements, endowed with global asymptotic stability guarantees. We then further propose a distributed velocity-free hybrid feedback control scheme that uses relative and absolute pose measurements, without requiring group velocity measurements, while preserving global asymptotic stability. Numerical simulations are presented to demonstrate the performance of the proposed distributed hybrid control schemes.

title: Safe Performance-aware Online Input Design
abstract: In this paper, we propose an input design framework for the safe online excitation and identification of uncertain linear systems without requiring informative initial data. The objective is to actively excite the system and collect sufficiently informative input-output data while maintaining safe operation and satisfactory control performance. Achieving this objective is challenging due to the potential conflict between the excitation required for learning and the safety and performance requirements, particularly when limited prior knowledge of the system is available. Inspired by the dual control principle, the proposed scheme balances exploitation for control performance with exploration for model improvement. A Bayesian learning approach is employed to update the model uncertainty online, starting from a conservative initial uncertainty set. As informative data are collected, the uncertainty set contracts, enabling progressively less conservative operation. To reduce the online computational burden, the resulting program is reformulated into a computationally tractable form. Furthermore, an online ellipsoidal terminal set with non-increasing conservatism is designed to guarantee the recursive feasibility of the proposed scheme. Numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, particularly in terms of uncertainty reduction and control performance.

title: Certified Zonotopic Reachability Analysis for Trajectory Tracking on Lie Groups
abstract: Autonomous vehicles track planned trajectories close to obstacles. Unknown disturbances make them deviate from these trajectories. With a bound on the tracking error that disturbances can cause, a planned trajectory can be certified as safe before execution. Existing set-based methods bound the tracking error by one invariant ellipsoid for the whole trajectory or by intervals, which are both conservative. For aerial and space vehicles, the tracking error evolves on a matrix Lie group with nonlinear dynamics. However, for group-affine systems, the error dynamics are linear in Lie algebra coordinates when the vehicle receives the inputs of the reference. The control input and the disturbance enter through the inverse right Jacobian, a matrix that depends on the error. We propagate the linear part of the error dynamics with zonotopes and enclose the effect of the inverse right Jacobian on the disturbance in closed form. The resulting tubes are tight and provably contain all reachable tracking errors in continuous time. When some error components have no input, the inverse right Jacobian leaves unmatched nonlinear terms in the closed loop. None of the tested methods certifies such a closed loop. Hybrid coordinates make these terms matched, so that our controller cancels every nonlinear term that does not contain the disturbance. Our tubes give tighter bounds than the ellipsoid method in simulations of a planar aircraft and a fully actuated multirotor and in real flights of a quadrotor, where the tube contains every measured attitude error. Under larger disturbances and the same feedback gain, the ellipsoid method yields no valid ellipsoid, whereas our tubes remain valid.

title: Succinct Infinite-Horizon Lyapunov and LQR Value Problems Are BQP-Complete
abstract: Fundamental tasks in linear systems analysis and control require evaluating infinite-horizon output energies for autonomous systems and optimal value functions for controlled systems. These quantities are characterized by Lyapunov and algebraic Riccati equations, respectively. In this work, we study promise problems for their evaluation when the system matrices are sparse and represented succinctly by Boolean circuits specifying their nonzero entries, with input length polynomial in the logarithm of the system dimension. For dissipative autonomous systems with coordinate-vector initial states, we define the succinct Lyapunov value problem (SLV). Its extension to linear-quadratic optimal control is the succinct LQR value problem (SLQRV). We prove that SLV is $\BQP$-hard: every problem in bounded-error quantum polynomial time ($\BQP$) reduces to it in polynomial time. We then establish that the more general SLQRV problem admits a quantum algorithm running in time polynomial in the succinct input length. Since SLV is a special case of SLQRV, both problems are $\BQP$-complete. Consequently, unless bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time coincides with $\BQP$, no classical randomized algorithm can solve either problem on all promised instances in time polynomial in the succinct input length.

title: Sliding into Balance: Benefits of a Sliding Payload for Load Distribution and Disturbance Rejection in Dual-UAV Transportation
abstract: This paper analyzes the cooperative transportation of a payload suspended from two drones in which, instead of being attached to two independent ropes, the payload is allowed to slide along a single rope connecting both UAVs. First, a planar nondimensional dynamical model of the sliding motion with viscous friction is presented. Then, considering stationary drones, this configuration is compared with a fixed payload with the same total rope length, both at equilibrium and under disturbances. The analytical results show that the sliding payload equalizes the tension in both rope segments for any relative position of the drones, so that no rope loses tension at equilibrium; it doubles the region reachable by the payload and, except for low friction combined with a large drone separation, it enlarges the set of admissible disturbances. Finally, a dynamic simulation also shows that under realistic gusty wind profiles, the average tension imbalance between the drones is reduced with respect to the fixed-payload solution.

title: The dimension of multi-index assignment polytopes and Latin-square transversal polytopes, via association schemes
abstract: We determine the dimensions, and the implicit equations, of several polytopes from integer programming whose vertices are the largest stable sets of highly symmetric graphs. Our main tools are two new dimension formulae within Lee's spectral method, which reads the dimension off of an association scheme: for amorphic schemes it becomes a threshold formula, and for point sets in $GF(q)^d$ invariant under the maps $z\mapsto az+b$ it is $q-1$ times the number of hyperplane directions along which some point is not equidistributed. A single integer point, a witness, then certifies a whole eigenspace. For the multi-index assignment polytopes of Appa, Magos, and Mourtos at prime-power orders, the dimension equals that of the linear relaxation except in two infinite families, which are, to our knowledge, the first counterexamples to their expectation that the two always coincide. The missing equations are explicit clique equations that the standard integer-programming formulation omits. For every abelian group with a transversal, the Latin-square transversal polytope of its Cayley table, equivalently the polytope of rainbow perfect matchings of the corresponding edge-colored $K_{n,n}$ , has the maximal dimension ${(n-1)(n-2)}$; the witnesses come from new constructions of complete mappings. We also treat transversals of Desarguesian nets and the largest sets of symmetric $3\times3$ and $4\times4$ matrices over $GF(q)$ whose differences have rank at least $3$, of sizes $q^3$ and $q^5$.

title: Adaptive Output Regulation of Linear Systems with Unknown Harmonic Exosystems and Additive Noise
abstract: This paper addresses error-feedback output regulation for known multivariable linear plants subject to an unknown exosystem and additive Gaussian process and measurement noise. The exosystem generates constant and sinusoidal signals, but its dimension, frequencies, and coupling matrices are unavailable. An output-injection transformation represents the external action through known channels. A causal observer then produces a residual independent of the applied input, whose filtered output separates into a harmonic signal, stationary colored Gaussian noise, and a decaying transient. Using this observation model, a Fourier procedure consistently identifies the number and values of the active positive frequencies in the presence of noise. The identified frequencies determine a regulator through interpolation with stable residual filters. A contractive filter realization, nonexpansive state resizing, and bounded gain updates ensure closed-loop moment bounds uniformly over the selected filter orders. If the gain bound contains the ideal interpolation gain, the adaptive plant response and tracking error converge in mean square to those of the corresponding known-frequency regulator. The limiting mean-square tracking error is a linear function of the process- and measurement-noise covariances. In the absence of both noises, the tracking error converges to zero.

title: Quantitative global regularity for Navier--Stokes equations with odd viscosity on the cubic three-torus
abstract: We study the three-dimensional incompressible Navier--Stokes equation on the cubic torus with a constant odd-viscosity operator given by the vertical derivative of the curl. Arbitrary real, mean-zero, divergence-free initial data and an independent steady force, both in the second-order Sobolev space, admit a unique global strong solution when the magnitude of one fixed odd-viscosity coefficient is at least a norm-uniform sufficient threshold. In the unforced case the solution is smooth at positive times. The qualitative argument adapts the resonant-averaging framework for rapidly rotating fluids to the different odd-viscous dispersion. Weighted lattice counts and signed corrected-energy estimates yield a sufficient bound for the odd-to-ordinary viscosity ratio that is polynomial in the normalized initial-data radius at each fixed normalized force radius, together with a separate bound in a specified force-dominated regime. No optimality is claimed for the polynomial exponents or prefactors; determining the sharp viscosity threshold for the original equation remains open. Direct kinetic and weighted enstrophy barriers also give regularity for every coefficient on explicit bounded data and force regions, including the closed unforced ball of homogeneous second-order Fourier Sobolev radius ninety-seven fortieths times the viscosity and seven closed forced rectangles. We specify how finite certificates enter the analytic argument and distinguish minimization of a sufficient formula from sharpness for the original equation. All three main theorems are formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib.

title: Efficient high-order Discontinuous Galerkin simulations of multi-species high-enthalpy flows
abstract: Numerical simulation of hypersonic vehicles is an attractive approach to investigate the complex phenomena involved in such technologies. For this, second-order finite volume methods (FVM) are the established method in computational fluid dynamics, with the cost of high dissipation in affordable meshes, thus needing refined ones or adaptive mesh refinements techniques to obtain accurate results. An alternative is to make use of high-order discontinuous Galerkin methods, in particular discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method (DGSEM), once it achieves higher formal order of accuracy on element-local polynomial bases. Therefore the goal of this work is to present the numerical simulations of a two-dimensional scramjet configuration to test and verify the applicability of the DGSEM approach for a complex hypersonic flow where shock-shock interactions occur. Results revealed to be in agreement with reference FVM solvers, thus verifying the code implementation.

title: N-Layer quasi-geostrophic modons in a vertically sheared flow
abstract: Modons, or dipolar vortices, are a form of propagating vortex solution consisting of two counterrotating regions of fluid and moving together under self-advection. They are common features of the upper ocean that can remain stable over long times, thereby transporting fluid over large distances. Here, we present a semi-analytical method for finding modon solutions in a vertically-sheared background flow using the multi-layer quasi-geostrophic framework. This method works for arbitrarily many fluid layers and builds on our previous studies of multi-layer modon solutions. We present three example of modons in a background flow, highlighting the effect of varying relative potential velocity between layers and the impact of depth-dependent potential vorticity gradients arising from surface deformation and velocity shear.

title: Amortized Transport-Map Likelihoods for Hierarchical Inverse Problems with Application to Wetting
abstract: Hierarchical Bayesian models pool measurements, but with the forward model in the likelihood every posterior evaluation costs one forward solve per cell. To reduce this cost, we introduce a simulation-based inference framework in which a triangular transport-map likelihood, trained once per design, serves every cell. We apply it to infer wetting properties from photographs of a stable hole in a thin liquid film. The hole's radius depends, through the nonlinear Young-Laplace equation, on the contact angle and capillary length. One photograph gives rank-one information about them, so we pool many in a hierarchical model whose cells, each a substrate at one volume setting, share the apparatus geometry and the noise scale. A design fixes the number of substrates, the volume settings and the photographs per cell. The map's posteriors agree with direct sampling of the forward model in the wetting properties at a synthetic validation design, and less closely at a larger synthetic scaling design. At the validation design, simulation-based calibration detects no departure for any parameter. There, the map needs several hundred times fewer forward-model evaluations than direct sampling with a gradient-free ensemble sampler for a single posterior, and about five orders of magnitude fewer over a calibration study of 200 posteriors. On real photographs its posterior agrees with direct sampling and is consistent with the measured radii. Trained offline, the amortized map turns new photographs into a posterior with no forward solve. It is thus a major step toward measuring wetting properties in situ without disturbing the liquid.

title: Input and Horizon Dependent Structural Fidelity in Chunk Coupled Spiking Networks
abstract: A fixed structural edit can preserve a spike sequence under one input and change it under another. We study this dependence using statistics-preserving edge swaps, controlled inputs and finite-horizon parameter certificates. The original 125-chunk numerical model is tested on ten artificial graphs from three connection rules. Despite identical total external drive at every slot, global and focal inputs change the visibility of 4--13 of nineteen fixed swaps per graph. A paired homogeneous and heterogeneous leaky integrate-and-fire validation in brian2-atlas reuses three originals and extends observation from 30 to 300 ms under a constant background drive sufficient for isolated-cell firing. Heterogeneous short-window switching persists, but by 300 ms every tested swap differs from its reference, saturating the binary visibility readout. Fixed-support weight families provide a complementary regional guarantee. Positive certified intervals cover 4,308 of 4,320 LIF direction conditions and include distinct floating-point configurations. A post hoc comparison finds a long-window failure inside the short-window certified interval in 710 of 720 heterogeneous conditions; 394 of 829 direction pairs ordered under both matched-drive inputs change order at 300 ms. Input-specific filtering and threshold-margin scores retain useful ordering but degrade with horizon and do not consistently beat activity controls. Earlier temporal-error, paired-dose and unsuccessful structural-selection results delimit what these findings imply. Together, the evidence links input-conditioned structural effects to finite-horizon fidelity regions in two deterministic kernels, without establishing universal topology rankings, model compression or asymptotic robustness.

title: Consistent Mapping for Fluid Structure Interaction with Geometrically Nonlinear Isogeometric Beams
abstract: Isogeometric beam formulations provide an efficient reduced-dimensional representation of slender structures, combining accurate geometry and high-order continuity with few structural degrees of freedom. Their application to fluid--structure interaction (FSI) requires transferring motion and loads between the one-dimensional beam centerline and the surrounding fluid interface. While mapping strategies exist for conventional finite element beams, geometrically nonlinear isogeometric formulations require operators consistent with their spline-based kinematics and distinct descriptions of cross-sectional rotation. This work develops consistent beam-to-surface mappings for geometrically nonlinear isogeometric Bernoulli and Timoshenko beams in partitioned FSI. Fluid-interface points are attached to the beam in the reference configuration and reconstructed using the nonlinear kinematics of each formulation. Consistent linearization yields a configuration-dependent mapping operator whose transpose ensures work-conjugate load transfer. The formulations are verified through analytical deformation tests, convergence studies, and virtual-work checks, and evaluated in beam-based adaptations of the Mok and Turek--Hron benchmarks and the Goland wing flutter benchmark. The results confirm accurate interface reconstruction and work-conjugate load transfer under large deformations, while demonstrating the applicability of both beam formulations to coupled FSI problems.

title: Physics-informed neural networks in the small-data regime: A controlled comparison with classical PDE surrogates
abstract: Neural surrogates for engineering models are often trained on large collections of simulated solutions. We investigate whether physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can achieve accurate predictions from scarce labelled observations by incorporating governing equations and prescribed initial and boundary conditions. We introduce hierarchical loss weighting (H-PINN) and its gradient-direction-aware extension (HO-PINN), which adjust the emphasis on physical constraints according to higher-priority losses. Hierarchical PINNs are compared with Vanilla PINN, tuned gradient boosting, support-vector regression, and Gaussian-process regression on a heat equation and three heterogeneous two-phase-flow benchmarks. Experiments use 20--1000 labelled states and ten paired seeds. Each label is one coordinate--state observation, not a complete simulation. At least one PINN variant achieves the highest mean primary-target \(R^2\) in each interpolation and equation-assisted forecasting comparison at 20 and 50 labels. The advantage for water saturation persists across all tested budgets. Hierarchical weighting reduces variability across runs in selected settings. These results demonstrate that known physics can support accurate neural surrogate predictions from very few solution observations, at substantially higher fitting cost than the tested classical regressors.

title: Law-Invariant Operators for Stochastic Mechanics
abstract: A central objective in stochastic mechanics is to separate deterministic physical behavior from the probability laws governing uncertain inputs. While classical spectral approaches achieve this separation in linear settings, nonlinear responses introduce interactions beyond conventional second-order variability response functions (VRF). Inspired by the spirit of VRFs, this work establishes that, for a fixed physical system, uncertainty propagation is described by a law-invariant operator mapping input realizations to responses, governed by the underlying physics and the deterministic parameters of the system. Different probability laws affect the input sampling and resulting response statistics, but not the mapping operator. We establish this law invariance under complete, invertible coordinate transformations and develop complementary, Fourier, fixed-reference polynomial-chaos (PCE) and finite element method (FEM) transfer formulations. Fourier captures nonlinear cross-frequency interactions and recovers the classical VRF in the appropriate linear limit, PCE describes coupling among stochastic modes, while FEM expresses the deterministic inverse-stiffness action. Neural approximations of these deterministic operators are investigated through analytical and finite-element benchmarks, examining cross-law generalization, the influence of training distributions and stochastic excitation, and the prediction of response fields and statistics. The results demonstrate the potential for reusing learned physical operators across different stochastic laws without retraining, while highlighting the importance of adequate training coverage and the challenges of accurately estimating low-probability events.

title: Physics-Informed Sinusoidal Representation Networks for Damage Identification in Ultrasonic Guided Wave Structural Health Monitoring
abstract: Ultrasonic guided wave (UGW) inspection has become an effective method in structural health monitoring (SHM). While machine learning has enhanced damage detection capabilities, purely data-driven models remain constrained by extensive labeled datasets and limited physical interpretability. Standard multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) further suffer from spectral bias (F-Principle) in high-frequency regimes, prioritizing low-frequency components while failing to resolve the high-frequency oscillations critical for UGW reconstruction. Physics-Informed Sinusoidal Representation Networks (PI-SIRENs) address these limitations by embedding governing partial differential equations directly into the training process. Building upon SIRENs, which utilize periodic activation functions to inherently capture high-frequency spectral content, the proposed framework is designed to operate effectively in sparse ultrasonic measurement regimes. This work introduces a frequency-domain PI-SIREN framework tailored for the Mindlin-Reissner plate theory to reconstruct ultrasonic wavefields without temporal discretization. The model parameters are optimized using a hybrid strategy comprising three phases: first-order Adam, residual-adaptive refinement (RAR) and quasi-Newton L-BFGS. Numerical and experimental evaluations confirm that the model serves as a physics-consistent baseline derived from sparse data, functioning as a computationally efficient surrogate for damage identification in SHM and non-destructive testing (NDT). Integrating the surrogate into a damage identification pipeline detects and localizes a milled notch from sparse experimental measurements with a localization error of 1 % of the plate diagonal. In contrast, data-driven benchmarks and MLPs with hyperbolic tangent activation functions, with and without Fourier feature embedding, are unable to identify damage due to higher reconstruction errors.
